title: System Design & Distributed Systems
tagline: Scalable architectures, distributed consensus, data partitioning, and high availability
description: Design systems that scale to millions of users: load balancers, database sharding, consistent hashing, message brokers, caching tiers, CAP theorem tradeoffs, and fault tolerance.

stages.title: Stage 1: Scalability & Distributed Principles
stages.description: Vertical vs horizontal scaling, latency numbers every programmer should know, and the CAP theorem.

nodes.title: CAP Theorem & PACELC Tradeoffs
nodes.description: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance in distributed networks, expanded by PACELC (Latency vs Consistency in normal operation).
nodes.whyItMatters: In any distributed system, network partitions will occur. Choosing CP (Consistency) vs AP (Availability) dictates how your application behaves during network splits.

resources.title: A Primer on the CAP Theorem

keyTakeaways: You cannot choose CA in a distributed system; network partitions are an unavoidable reality of hardware.
CP systems (like etcd, CockroachDB) refuse stale writes/reads during network splits; AP systems (like Cassandra, DynamoDB) return available data that may be eventually consistent.
Understand eventual consistency, read-your-own-writes consistency, and monotonic read guarantees.
nodes.interviewTips: Interviewers will ask how you choose between Cassandra (AP) and Postgres/etcd (CP) for specific product features like chat vs banking ledger.

nodes.title: Load Balancing & Consistent Hashing
nodes.description: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 load balancers, health checks, algorithm strategies (round-robin, least connections), and Consistent Hashing rings.
nodes.whyItMatters: Standard modulo hashing (hash(key) % N) re-indexes 90%+ of keys whenever a server is added or removed, causing massive cache stampedes. Consistent Hashing minimizes remapping to 1/N.
keyTakeaways: Layer 4 load balancers route at the transport layer (TCP/UDP); Layer 7 inspects HTTP headers, cookies, and URL paths.
Consistent Hashing places nodes and keys on a virtual ring (0 to 2^32-1) with virtual nodes to balance load distribution uniformly.
Use health checks with active polling and circuit breakers to remove dead backend instances automatically.
nodes.interviewTips: Be prepared to draw a consistent hashing circle and demonstrate what happens when a node fails or is added.

stages.title: Stage 2: Storage Scaling & Partitioning
stages.description: Replication topologies, horizontal sharding, partition keys, and distributed transactions.

nodes.title: Database Sharding & Read Replication
nodes.description: Active-passive vs active-active replication, replication lag, choosing sharding keys, and cross-shard queries.
nodes.whyItMatters: When database storage or write IOPS exceeds the capacity of the largest single hardware node, sharding splits data across multiple independent database clusters.

resources.title: Sharding Pinterest: How we scaled to 50B pins

keyTakeaways: Pick a shard key with high cardinality and even distribution to prevent hot-spotting.
Avoid cross-shard joins; denormalize data or execute application-level scatter-gather queries.
Account for replication lag when directing reads to read-replicas immediately after a user write.
nodes.interviewTips: Classic interview question: How to scale a Twitter-like feed system (push vs pull fanout model).

stages.title: Stage 3: Resiliency & Distributed Consensus
stages.description: Saga pattern, Raft consensus, rate limiting algorithms, and disaster recovery.

nodes.title: Distributed Transactions: 2PC vs Saga Pattern
nodes.description: Why Two-Phase Commit (2PC) blocks in distributed microservices, and how the Saga pattern coordinates local transactions with compensating transactions.
nodes.whyItMatters: In microservices, a single business workflow (order -> payment -> inventory -> shipping) spans multiple databases. Sagas ensure eventual consistency without distributed locks.
keyTakeaways: Orchestration-based Sagas use a central orchestrator service; Choreography-based Sagas rely on event broadcasting.
Every action in a saga must have an inverse compensating action (e.g., refund payment if inventory reserve fails).
Design all steps to be idempotent to handle retried messages safely.
nodes.interviewTips: Interviewers will ask how to recover if the orchestrator crashes midway through a transaction or if a compensating transaction fails.
